fields.definition: A subjective term for a thin, buzzy, effervescent high-frequency character, typically excess energy in the upper treble and presence region (roughly 4-10 kHz), often heard on harshly distorted electric guitar or low-quality digital distortion.
fields.plain_english: Fizzy means the sound has a thin, buzzy edge up top, like the hiss of a soda. It usually comes from too much harsh treble, often on a distorted guitar.
fields.purpose_function: The term lets engineers quickly flag unpleasant, grainy top-end energy so it can be tamed with EQ or a different cabinet, mic, or distortion setting.
fields.practical_application: A tech hearing a fizzy guitar tone might roll off upper treble with EQ, swap the speaker cabinet or mic position, or reduce the amount of gain and distortion.
common_mistakes: Confusing fizzy (thin, buzzy treble) with gritty (rough mid-range dirt)
Adding more presence or treble EQ to a fizzy tone, which makes it worse
Assuming fizz is always the amp when mic choice and placement often cause it
scenario_contexts: A high-gain electric guitar that sounds buzzy and thin in a mix
Cheap digital distortion or amp-sim plugins adding harsh top end
An overhead or cymbal track with brittle, effervescent high frequencies

fields.definition: A subjective term for loose, poorly controlled, ill-defined low-frequency reproduction that lacks tightness and damping, so bass notes sound soft, boomy, and slow rather than firm and articulate.
fields.plain_english: Flabby means the bass sounds loose and soft, with no firm edge. It is like a drum with a slack head that thuds instead of hitting cleanly.
fields.purpose_function: The term flags bass that lacks control or definition, prompting fixes in damping, EQ, speaker or room setup, or playing technique.
fields.practical_application: A tech may tighten a flabby low end by cutting a boomy frequency region, improving room treatment, or checking loudspeaker damping and port tuning.
common_mistakes: Boosting bass EQ to fix flabbiness, which makes it looser
Blaming the source when room modes cause the flab
Confusing flabby (loose bass) with full (rich, strong bass)
scenario_contexts: A bass guitar or kick drum with loose, undefined low end
Loudspeakers in an untreated room with strong bass build-up
A ported speaker or subwoofer tuned poorly, giving soft, slow bass

fields.definition: A subjective term for soft, loose, undefined low-frequency character with weak transient definition, especially a kick drum or bass that sounds spongy and lacks punch or attack.
fields.plain_english: Flubby means the low notes sound soft and spongy, with no punch. A flubby kick drum goes 'flub' instead of a tight thump.
fields.purpose_function: The term identifies a lack of attack and control in the low end so it can be tightened for clarity and punch.
fields.practical_application: A tech might tighten a flubby kick with EQ, gating, better tuning or muffling, or by adjusting compressor attack to restore punch.
common_mistakes: Adding low-end EQ to a flubby kick instead of tightening it
Ignoring drum tuning or muffling, which often causes flub
Confusing flubby (soft, no punch) with punchy (tight, strong attack)
scenario_contexts: A kick drum that sounds soft and lacks thump in a mix
An over-resonant bass note that blooms and loses definition
A poorly tuned or undamped tom sounding loose and spongy

fields.definition: A subjective term for sound that is tight, coherent, and well-defined, with clear imaging and energy concentrated in a precise location rather than smeared or diffuse.
fields.plain_english: Focused means the sound is tight and clear, and you can tell exactly where it sits. It is like a sharp photo instead of a blurry one.
fields.purpose_function: The term describes strong definition and precise imaging, a goal when aligning, EQ-ing, or positioning sources so each one sits clearly.
fields.practical_application: A tech aims for a focused image by time-aligning speakers, clearing masking frequencies, and controlling reflections so instruments sound tight and placed.
common_mistakes: Thinking louder equals more focused, when clarity comes from definition
Over-narrowing EQ and losing natural body while chasing focus
Confusing focused (tight, defined) with forward (close, prominent)
scenario_contexts: A well-time-aligned PA where each instrument sits clearly
A vocal that sits precisely in the center of a mix
A tightly EQ-ed drum bus with clear, defined transients

fields.definition: A subjective term for sound that appears close and prominent to the listener, seeming to sit in front of the mix, often from emphasis in the upper-midrange and presence region (roughly 1-5 kHz).
fields.plain_english: Forward means the sound feels close and up-front, like someone stepping toward you to speak. It often comes from a lift in the upper-middle frequencies.
fields.purpose_function: The term describes a source's front-to-back position, guiding how prominent or intimate an instrument or voice sits in a mix.
fields.practical_application: A tech can push a vocal forward with a presence boost, level, and compression, or pull it back by reducing upper mids and adding reverb.
common_mistakes: Confusing forward (close, prominent) with bright (extra treble)
Pushing everything forward, so nothing stands out
Using only level to make a source forward, ignoring EQ presence
scenario_contexts: A lead vocal that sits close and up-front in a pop mix
A guitar with a presence boost that jumps out of the speakers
A microphone with a presence peak making a voice sound immediate

fields.definition: A subjective term for a rich, weighty sound with strong low-frequency and low-midrange content, giving a sense of body and completeness across the spectrum.
fields.plain_english: Full means the sound has plenty of body and weight, with strong lows. It is the opposite of thin, like a big, solid wall of sound with real weight behind it.
fields.purpose_function: The term describes tonal weight and body, guiding EQ and arrangement choices to make a source or mix sound complete rather than thin.
fields.practical_application: A tech may add fullness with low-mid EQ, layering, or mic choice, while watching that it does not tip into muddy or boomy.
common_mistakes: Overdoing low-mid EQ, turning full into muddy
Confusing full (rich body) with simply loud
Thinking only bass makes a sound full, ignoring low mids
scenario_contexts: A vocal that sounds rich and complete rather than thin
A mix with strong low-mid body and weight
Choosing a large-diaphragm mic to add fullness to a voice

fields.definition: A subjective term for a bright, clear, hard-edged high-frequency character that sounds smooth yet reflective and slightly brittle, like the surface of glass, usually in the upper treble.
fields.plain_english: Glassy means the top end is very bright and clear, with a hard, shiny edge. It sounds smooth but can feel brittle, like tapping a glass.
fields.purpose_function: The term flags a hard, reflective top end so it can be used for clarity and sparkle or softened when it becomes brittle or fatiguing.
fields.practical_application: A tech might smooth a glassy top with a gentle high-shelf cut or de-essing, or keep it for sparkle on a clean electric piano or guitar.
common_mistakes: Confusing glassy (hard, bright top) with warm
Boosting a high shelf on an already glassy source
Assuming glassy always sounds good, when it can be brittle and tiring
scenario_contexts: A clean electric piano such as a Rhodes or DX with a bright, shiny top
A chime or bell with a hard, reflective high end
A vocal recorded through a bright condenser sounding glassy

fields.definition: A subjective term for a sense of cohesion that makes separate mix elements sound like one unified whole; commonly achieved with gentle bus compression (often called 'glue compression') and shared processing.
fields.plain_english: Glue is when all the parts of a mix feel like they belong together, not like separate pieces. Gentle compression across the whole mix helps bind them, like tying a bundle together.
fields.purpose_function: Glue helps a mix sound cohesive and finished, so instruments feel connected rather than like isolated tracks stacked on top of each other.
fields.practical_application: A mix engineer often applies slow-attack, low-ratio bus compression, shared reverb, or subtle saturation across a group bus to add glue.
common_mistakes: Over-compressing the bus, which crushes dynamics instead of gluing
Thinking glue is a single plugin rather than a result of cohesion
Confusing glue (cohesion) with loudness
scenario_contexts: Adding gentle compression across a mix bus to bind a mix
Using a shared drum-bus compressor to make a kit sound like one instrument
Applying subtle saturation to make layered tracks feel connected

fields.definition: A subjective term for a rough, textured, slightly distorted character caused by added harmonic distortion or edge, giving a sound dirt and aggression without being fully clean.
fields.plain_english: Gritty means the sound has a rough, dirty texture, like sandpaper. It comes from a bit of distortion that adds edge and attitude.
fields.purpose_function: The term describes deliberate roughness or harmonic edge, used to add energy and character, or flagged when it is unwanted.
fields.practical_application: A tech may add grit with saturation, overdrive, or a driven preamp for character, or reduce it by backing off gain when it becomes harsh.
common_mistakes: Confusing gritty (rough mid texture) with fizzy (thin, buzzy treble)
Adding grit until it becomes harsh and fatiguing
Assuming grit needs treble, when it is mostly harmonic distortion
scenario_contexts: An overdriven bass or guitar with rough, dirty texture
A vocal run through saturation for edge and attitude
A driven preamp or tape emulation adding gritty character
